cases.title: The gene clue that changed melanoma research
cases.intro: Follow how a gene change became a testable treatment idea, and what a later randomized trial could—and could not—establish.
cases.hook: Could a change in a tumor's DNA reveal a weakness worth testing?

chapters.title: Researchers found a recurring DNA clue.
chapters.body: A 2002 study reported BRAF mutations in 66% of the malignant melanoma specimens it examined. That was a finding in that study, not a claim about every melanoma in the world.
chapters.takeaway: First locate the finding and the population actually studied.

chapters.title: What might the mutation be doing?
chapters.body: BRAF participates in a signaling pathway affecting cell growth. A mutation can alter that pathway. Researchers could ask whether some tumor cells depended on the altered signal.
chapters.takeaway: A molecular explanation creates a hypothesis; it is not yet clinical proof.

chapters.title: Compare responses in a randomized study.
chapters.body: A 2011 trial compared vemurafenib with dacarbazine in people with previously untreated advanced BRAF V600-mutant melanoma. Among patients evaluable for tumor response, confirmed responses were reported in 48% versus 5%, respectively.
chapters.takeaway: Read the methods and denominator before interpreting percentages.

chapters.title: A strong result still has boundaries.
chapters.body: The trial showed important benefits in the studied population, but a response does not mean every patient benefits or that the disease is cured. Treatment evidence and practice have continued evolving since 2011.
chapters.takeaway: Scientific advances must be interpreted in the precise context they were tested.

cases.tool_why: Open Targets lets researchers explore public evidence connecting genes, biological functions, and diseases. This is a modern exploration tool, not what the original investigators used in 2002.
cases.tool_task: Open the modern BRAF target page. Find its gene description and evidence links. Identify one disease association and note that it does not itself prove a treatment works.
cases.tool_answer: BRAF is a protein-coding gene involved in the MAPK signaling pathway. An evidence association is a starting point, not a patient-response prediction.
cases.tool_limitation: A research database is not a clinical recommendation. The 2011 drug comparison is historical and modern melanoma treatment options have evolved.
